title: Relevance-ordered record sequencing (foundational)
description: Selected records are ordered by relevance score, most relevant first, because models attend more strongly to early context. Ties break by recency so fresher records win. The ordering is stable and deterministic for a given score set, which makes assembled contexts reproducible. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
recs = [('r1', 0.6, '2026-10-18'), ('r2', 0.9, '2026-10-10'), ('r3', 0.9, '2026-10-20')]
ordered = sorted(recs, key=lambda r: (r[1], r[2]), reverse=True)
print('assembly order:', [r[0] for r in ordered])
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Long-Context Assembly Engine practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Token budget allocation per record (foundational)
description: The total token budget is split across records proportionally to relevance, with a minimum floor so no selected record is starved to zero. Proportional allocation spends the most tokens where they matter most instead of giving every record an equal slice. The floor guarantees each record contributes at least its headline facts. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
recs = [('r1', 0.9), ('r2', 0.6), ('r3', 0.3)]
BUDGET, FLOOR = 1000, 100
tot = sum(s for _, s in recs)
alloc = {r: FLOOR + int((BUDGET - FLOOR * len(recs)) * s / tot) for r, s in recs}
print('token allocation:', alloc, 'total:', sum(alloc.values()))
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Long-Context Assembly Engine practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Coherence stitching with source markers (foundational)
description: Records are joined with lightweight source markers like '[r2]' so the model can attribute each span to its record. Markers prevent the classic long-context failure where facts from different records blend into one false memory. The stitching adds no commentary of its own, keeping the context purely sourced. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
recs = [('r1', 'archive holds 52,268 databases'), ('r2', 'growth is daily')]
ctx = '\n'.join(f'[{r}] {t}' for r, t in recs)
print(ctx)
print('attribution preserved:', '[r1]' in ctx and '[r2]' in ctx)
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Long-Context Assembly Engine practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

t: Truncation policy: tail-cut with headline keep (foundational)
title: Truncation policy: tail-cut with headline keep (foundational)
description: When a record exceeds its allocation, it is truncated from the tail but its first sentence, the headline, is always kept. Headlines carry the record's main claim, so tail-cutting loses detail before it loses meaning. The truncation point is recorded so readers know the record continues beyond what is shown. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
demo:
text = 'Headline: counts verified. Detail one. Detail two. Detail three. Detail four.'
limit = 40
head, rest = text.split('. ', 1)
out = head + '. ' + rest[:max(0, limit - len(head))] + '... [truncated]'
print(out)
print('headline kept:', out.startswith('Headline'))
provenance: Public computer-science methods literature (Long-Context Assembly Engine practice); cross-checked against standard references, 2026-10-21.

title: Assembled context validation (foundational)
description: The finished context is validated: total tokens within budget, every selected record present at least as a headline, and source markers well-formed. Validation failures trigger re-assembly with adjusted allocations rather than shipping a broken context. The validator's report travels with the context so downstream steps can see what was included and cut. Foundational form: the core technique demonstrated on a minimal example.
